case_analysis.focal_point: Whether an appellate court may affirm a judgment (or otherwise resolve an appeal) on a legal theory not properly preserved below—treating the issue as a “pure matter of law” with a “certain” outcome—or whether ordinary forfeiture/waiver principles bar considering that newly presented legal argument.
case_analysis.legal_provision: No single statute is identified in the excerpts provided; the dispute instead centers on federal appellate preservation doctrines (forfeiture/waiver) and the scope of appellate discretion to consider unpreserved questions of law, as reflected in federal common-law standards applied by the Tenth Circuit.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that the Tenth Circuit (or the court below) improperly entertained and resolved the case based on a legal argument that was forfeited (not timely raised/preserved), and that allowing courts to decide cases on newly presented theories undermines adversarial testing, fairness, and orderly procedure; they contend the Supreme Court should enforce stricter preservation rules and reject the “pure matter of law / certain resolution” exception as applied (or narrow it).
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent argues that the appellate court properly exercised discretion to consider the issue because it presents a purely legal question whose correct resolution is clear (i.e., beyond reasonable doubt), making remand or strict enforcement of forfeiture unnecessary; respondent emphasizes that appellate courts have long recognized limited circumstances where considering a forfeited legal argument serves accuracy and judicial economy without prejudicing the parties.

Ave. Cap. Mgmt. II, L.P. v. Schaden, 843 F.3d 876 (10th Cir.)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is efficiency: Singleton and Hormel do recognize discretion to reach a purely legal issue on an adequate record to avoid a pointless remand. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor stress, that discretion is framed as exceptional and fairness-rooted, and the Tenth Circuit’s “certainty/beyond reasonable doubt” gloss risks turning a prudential safety valve into an administrable rule that invites appellate courts to decide untested theories without full adversarial development. Thomas and Gorsuch rightly underscore the structural role of preservation in constraining judicial power and maintaining the party-presentation model, which is central to institutional legitimacy. A minimal, legitimacy-protecting disposition is to reverse and reaffirm the default preservation rule while leaving only genuinely unusual cases—adequate record, no prejudice, and truly indisputable law—to the traditional narrow exception described in Singleton and Hormel.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is that Singleton and Hormel recognize appellate discretion to reach a purely legal issue on an adequate record to avoid a pointless remand, and that a “certainty” requirement supposedly cabins that discretion. But as the Chief Justice notes, Singleton describes a prudential, case-specific judgment grounded in fairness and the ordinary rule of party presentation, not a freestanding “inevitable result” doctrine; converting discretion into an administrable certainty test risks expanding appellate power beyond its traditional bounds. From an originalist and textualist perspective, preservation and forfeiture rules reflect settled limits on the judicial role in our adversarial system, and departures must remain truly exceptional and tied to demonstrable lack of prejudice and full record development—not an appellate court’s post hoc confidence. Justice Gorsuch’s concern that a routinized certainty standard undermines incentives to litigate issues in the trial court reinforces that this approach threatens the structural functions of preservation.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: I take the Chief Justice’s and Justice Kagan’s point that preservation serves fairness, adversarial testing, and institutional legitimacy, and that a court’s asserted “certainty” can be impressionistic. But Singleton v. Wulff and Hormel do not impose a categorical bar; they recognize a narrow appellate discretion where the issue is purely legal, the record is complete, and insisting on forfeiture would simply force a pointless remand. Justice Gorsuch’s invocation of Olano underscores that discretion should be constrained, yet Olano’s caution about forfeiture is compatible with a truly cabined exception when the legal result is inevitable and no additional factfinding could matter. In my view, the Tenth Circuit’s “certain/beyond reasonable doubt” framing—properly applied—does not swallow the rule; it is a demanding way to operationalize the exceptional-case discretion already recognized in our precedents while avoiding unnecessary delay and cost.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito’s judicial-economy point has bite only if “certainty” reliably signals that adversarial testing and record development would add nothing, but Singleton and Hormel treat that as a fairness-based, truly exceptional discretion—not a rule that turns on an appellate court’s after-the-fact confidence. As the Chief Justice emphasizes, a routinized “certain outcome” gloss invites appellate courts to decide cases on theories the parties never had reason or resources to litigate below, and that systemic tilt predictably harms less-resourced litigants and undermines access to justice. Justice Kagan’s point that preservation structures incentives and the record underscores why “purely legal” often isn’t apparent until the new theory is explored; what looks inevitable on appeal may rest on untested factual predicates or legal assumptions. I would reverse and sharply narrow the Tenth Circuit’s Jarvis/Avenue Capital formulation: absent an adequate record, clear lack of prejudice, and genuinely indisputable law, courts should not affirm on an unpreserved theory.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s judicial-economy point has intuitive pull, but his reliance on “certainty” as the cabining principle still misreads Singleton and Hormel as closer to a rule than a prudential, fairness-rooted discretion. As the Chief Justice explains, preservation is structural: it shapes the record and the parties’ incentives, and an appellate court’s after-the-fact confidence can’t substitute for adversarial testing of a theory never litigated below. Even accepting that some cases present an adequate record and an indisputable legal answer, endorsing the Tenth Circuit’s Jarvis/Avenue Capital gloss risks normalizing affirmance on newly minted theories and thereby eroding the default preservation regime. The administrable middle ground is to reaffirm the default rule and reserve deviation for truly unusual circumstances with demonstrable lack of prejudice—something “certainty” alone does not ensure.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is that Singleton and Hormel recognize discretion to reach a forfeited, purely legal issue to avoid needless remands when the record is adequate. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas emphasize, those cases describe a narrow, prudential exception anchored in fairness to the parties and the adversarial system—not an administrable alternative keyed to appellate “certainty,” which risks converting discretion into a routinized bypass around preservation. Even a “beyond reasonable doubt” label does not solve the structural problem: absent presentation below, we cannot reliably know whether the issue is truly “purely legal,” whether factual predicates might have mattered, or whether the opponent was deprived of meaningful notice and opportunity to contest the theory. Olano’s framework reinforces that forfeiture constrains appellate review to preserve the primacy of party presentation and the trial forum, so I would reverse and reject the Tenth Circuit’s broader certainty-based formulation except in truly extraordinary, demonstrably nonprejudicial circumstances.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito’s judicial-economy point—grounded in Singleton and Hormel—has real appeal when an issue is purely legal and the record seems complete, but those cases frame appellate consideration of unpreserved issues as a prudential, exceptional practice keyed to fairness and record adequacy, not a generally administrable “certainty” test. As Chief Justice Roberts stresses, preservation rules serve structural and legitimacy interests (party presentation, notice, and factual development), and a “beyond reasonable doubt/certain outcome” standard (Jarvis/Avenue Capital) risks converting discretion into a routinized bypass that invites appellate courts to declare inevitability without adversarial testing. Even if some cases truly are inevitable, the better institutional rule is to enforce forfeiture absent unusual circumstances showing a fully developed record and clear lack of prejudice—conditions not reliably ensured by an appellate court’s post hoc confidence. On that understanding of Singleton/Hormel, I would reverse the affirmance on the unpreserved theory and, if necessary, remand for proper consideration.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s appeal to Singleton’s prudential discretion and judicial economy is the strongest argument for Respondent, but Singleton and Hormel describe a narrow, fairness-anchored departure from preservation—not a standard that turns on an appellate court’s post hoc “certainty” about a newly advanced theory. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, that discretion is exceptional and depends on adequate record development and the absence of prejudice; those predicates are precisely what becomes difficult to verify when the theory was never litigated below. Even the Tenth Circuit’s “beyond reasonable doubt” formulation (Jarvis/Avenue Capital) is administratively unstable because “certainty” often masks untested factual or legal disputes that proper adversarial presentation would surface. Under a party-presentation, original-public-meaning understanding of appellate review, I would enforce forfeiture here and reverse.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—endorsed as a matter of efficiency—is that Singleton and Hormel allow discretion to reach a purely legal, outcome-determinative issue and avoid needless remands when the result is “certain.” But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, those precedents ground the exception in prudential fairness (adequate adversarial testing, an adequate record, and lack of prejudice), not in appellate judges’ post hoc confidence; a “certainty” gloss risks eroding preservation by incentivizing strategic forfeiture and by masking factual/legal contestability that only emerges when the theory is litigated. From a progressive-pragmatist perspective attentive to real-world consequences, relaxing forfeiture in this way predictably burdens less-resourced litigants and increases error by encouraging appellate resolution on underdeveloped records. Because the record here does not sufficiently assure no prejudice or truly indisputable law, I would reverse and reaffirm that only unusual, fairness-justified circumstances permit affirmance on an unpreserved theory.

John Roberts.reasoning: Ordinary preservation rules are critical to the adversarial process and to institutional legitimacy, and we have repeatedly treated forfeiture/waiver as the default rule rather than a mere suggestion. Under Hormel v. Helvering, 312 U.S. 552 (1941), appellate consideration of issues not raised below is at most a limited exception, justified only in unusual circumstances (e.g., to avoid manifest injustice or when the issue is truly beyond dispute), not a general license to affirm on a newly minted theory. The Tenth Circuit’s “pure matter of law / certain outcome” approach risks becoming a broad carveout that invites appellate courts to decide cases on untested theories, undermining fair notice and orderly procedure. A narrow ruling enforcing preservation here best respects precedent and keeps appellate review within its proper bounds.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The traditional rule of appellate review is that parties must present their arguments in the trial court, and forfeiture/waiver doctrines serve structural purposes rooted in the adversarial system and the limited role of appellate courts. Although Hormel v. Helvering, 312 U.S. 552 (1941), recognized narrow discretion to consider issues not raised below, it described that discretion as exceptional and justified only where “injustice might otherwise result,” not as a broad “pure matter of law/certain outcome” license. The Tenth Circuit’s formulation in United States v. Jarvis and Ave. Cap. Mgmt. II v. Schaden risks expanding appellate power beyond its proper bounds by inviting courts to decide unpreserved legal theories without full factual development and adversarial testing. Consistent with limited judicial power and orderly procedure, I would hold ordinary forfeiture principles control absent truly extraordinary circumstances.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Appellate courts have long possessed discretion to consider issues not passed upon below when the question is purely legal and the correct result is clear, a limited practice recognized in Singleton v. Wulff, 428 U.S. 106 (1976). The Tenth Circuit’s formulation in United States v. Jarvis, 499 F.3d 1196 (10th Cir. 2007), as tightened by Ave. Cap. Mgmt. II, L.P. v. Schaden, 843 F.3d 876 (10th Cir.), is consistent with that tradition by requiring that the proper disposition be “certain” or “beyond reasonable doubt,” which mitigates fairness concerns and avoids unnecessary remands. Strict forfeiture rules serve important adversarial and procedural interests, but where the outcome is legally inevitable, refusing to consider the issue elevates form over substance and imposes needless costs. Given the narrowness of the exception and its focus on accuracy and judicial economy, I would affirm the appellate court’s discretion to resolve the appeal on that unpreserved legal theory in this limited circumstance.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Ordinary forfeiture principles generally bar an appellate court from deciding a case on a legal theory not properly preserved below, because doing so deprives the opposing party of adversarial testing and can work concrete unfairness—especially to parties with fewer resources or less sophisticated counsel. Singleton v. Wulff recognizes limited appellate discretion to consider issues not raised, but it cautions that such discretion should be exercised sparingly and with attention to fairness and the need for an adequate record. The Tenth Circuit’s “pure matter of law / certain resolution” exception (Jarvis; Ave. Cap. Mgmt. II) risks becoming an end-run around preservation where “certainty” is debatable and the record and briefing were shaped by different theories. Given the systemic and practical costs to access to justice and procedural regularity, I would require stricter adherence to preservation and reject (or substantially narrow) affirmance on a forfeited theory here.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Ordinary forfeiture principles generally bar parties from pressing new legal theories on appeal, and our cases treat any departure as a narrow, discretionary exception grounded in fairness to the opposing party and the benefits of full adversarial testing. Singleton v. Wulff and Hormel v. Helvering allow consideration of unpreserved issues only in limited circumstances—typically when the issue is truly a pure question of law, the record is adequate, and deciding it will not prejudice the parties or undermine orderly procedure. The Tenth Circuit’s “pure matter of law / certain outcome” gloss (Jarvis; Ave. Cap. Mgmt.) cannot become an all-purpose bypass around preservation, especially where the unraised theory could have been litigated below and where “certainty” is contestable. A workable middle ground is to enforce forfeiture absent exceptional circumstances, preserving appellate flexibility while maintaining coherent, predictable procedure.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Ordinary preservation rules reflect the adversarial system and the judiciary’s limited role: appellate courts generally should not decide cases on theories the parties did not press and the trial court did not pass upon, absent a recognized and narrowly confined exception. Olano distinguishes waiver from forfeiture and underscores that even when an issue is merely forfeited, appellate consideration is discretionary and constrained, not a license to recast the case on appeal. The Tenth Circuit’s “pure matter of law/certain outcome” formulation in Jarvis and Avenue Capital risks diluting forfeiture principles by inviting appellate courts to resolve unpreserved theories based on their own certainty, rather than on proper presentation and testing below. Respect for procedural regularity and separation of powers counsels enforcing forfeiture here and requiring parties to preserve the legal theory in the district court (or else satisfy stringent plain-error-type limits).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Ordinary forfeiture/waiver principles generally bar a party from prevailing on a new legal theory first advanced on appeal because preservation promotes adversarial testing, fairness to the opposing party, and orderly procedure. Although Singleton v. Wulff, 428 U.S. 106 (1976), recognizes limited appellate discretion to consider issues not raised below, it describes that power as exceptional and grounded in prudential concerns, not a routine “pure question of law” escape hatch. The Tenth Circuit’s formulation in United States v. Jarvis and Ave. Capital Management II (allowing consideration only when the legal issue is “pure” and the outcome “certain/beyond reasonable doubt”) still risks undermining workability and incentives to properly preserve arguments; absent truly extraordinary circumstances or clear lack of prejudice, the safer institutional course is to enforce forfeiture and remand if necessary. Respect for precedent and practical administrability therefore favors tightening use of the exception and rejecting its application here if the theory was not properly preserved.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Ordinary preservation rules reflect core features of the adversarial system and are not lightly displaced: under United States v. Olano, forfeiture is the failure to timely assert a right, and appellate courts may correct forfeited issues only within constrained discretion, not as a routine alternative ground for affirmance. The Tenth Circuit’s “pure matter of law”/“certain outcome” exception (Jarvis; Ave. Cap. Mgmt. II) underscores that discretion is narrow and turns on whether the correct legal disposition is beyond reasonable doubt—conditions that are typically absent when the new theory is contested or implicates unresolved legal questions. Allowing affirmance on an unpreserved legal theory risks unfair surprise and deprives the district court and opposing party of proper development and testing, which is precisely what forfeiture doctrine is designed to prevent. Consistent with Olano’s methodological limits and the ordinary rule that a party may not switch theories on appeal (see Lone Star Steel), I would enforce forfeiture here and reject reliance on the newly presented legal argument.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Appellate courts generally should not affirm on a theory not preserved below because doing so undermines the party-presentation principle and deprives the opposing party of adversarial testing and a fair opportunity to build a record, concerns this Court emphasized in Singleton v. Wulff, 428 U.S. 106 (1976). The Tenth Circuit’s “pure matter of law / certain outcome” exception (Jarvis; Ave. Cap. Mgmt. II) is at most a narrow discretion and should not be used to bypass ordinary forfeiture/waiver rules absent truly extraordinary clarity and lack of prejudice. From a procedural-fairness and practical-consequences perspective—especially in contexts with asymmetries in litigation resources—strict preservation better promotes accuracy and legitimacy than appellate resolution on newly minted legal theories. Because the newly presented argument was forfeited and its consideration risks unfairness and error, the judgment should not be affirmed on that basis.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a federal appellate court may treat a party’s newly raised appellate statutory-interpretation theory as forfeited and decline to consider it (or, alternatively, must consider it) when it presents a purportedly “pure question of law” whose resolution is claimed to be clear, in a case arising from a worker-classification dispute involving Flowers Foods and a delivery driver.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure and judge-made forfeiture/waiver doctrines governing issue preservation on appeal (as applied by the Tenth Circuit); the underlying substantive worker-protection/employment statute(s) implicated by the classification dispute (not specified in the provided excerpts).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (Flowers Foods, Inc., et al.) argue that the Tenth Circuit improperly refused to consider a dispositive legal argument on appeal on the ground that it was forfeited, and that where an issue is a “pure matter of law” with a certain (or beyond-reasonable-doubt) correct resolution, an appellate court should reach it to avoid an erroneous judgment and to ensure uniform application of federal law; petitioners’ amici supporting them frame the issue as important to appellate administration and to defendants facing high-stakes statutory and employment-liability exposure.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent (Angelo Brock) argues that the Tenth Circuit correctly applied standard preservation principles: parties must present their legal theories in the district court, and appellate courts may (and often should) decline to entertain newly presented legal arguments except in narrow, clearly satisfied circumstances; respondent’s amici emphasize that relaxing forfeiture rules would encourage sandbagging, undermine fair notice and factual development, and disproportionately harm workers in employment and misclassification disputes.
key_precedents: United States v. Jarvis, 499 F.3d 1196 (10th Cir. 2007)
Ave. Cap. Mgmt. II, L.P. v. Schaden, 843 F.3d 876 (10th Cir.)

John Roberts.reasoning: The petitioners’ strongest contention—that statutory interpretation is a “pure question of law” that an appellate court must reach to ensure the correct rule—fails under Singleton v. Wulff and Hormel v. Helvering, which treat consideration of issues not raised below as a prudential, fairness-and-administration discretion rather than a categorical entitlement. Justice Jackson’s emphasis on fairness and the adversarial process underscores that even “legal” reframings can prejudice the other side by shifting what facts mattered and how the case was litigated, so a mandatory exception would undercut preservation and invite sandbagging. Justice Kagan’s point that the Tenth Circuit’s “certain/beyond reasonable doubt” threshold functions as an administrable safety valve persuades me we can affirm on narrow grounds without announcing any rigid rule beyond confirming appellate discretion. Nothing in the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure, as Justice Thomas notes, displaces that traditional discretion or converts it into an obligation.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point—that a newly raised statutory-interpretation theory is a “pure question of law” and therefore must be reached—still lacks any footing in the Constitution’s text, the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure, or our tradition of party presentation. As Chief Justice Roberts explains, Singleton v. Wulff makes clear that considering issues not raised below is ordinarily discretionary, and Justice Jackson’s reliance on Hormel v. Helvering does not convert that discretion into an obligation; Hormel recognizes limited equitable leeway, not a categorical entitlement. Justice Kagan’s administrability concern underscores why an automatic “pure law” exception would invite sandbagging and erode preservation doctrine by encouraging litigants to re-label mixed questions as legal ones. Because the Tenth Circuit’s “certainty/beyond reasonable doubt” threshold is simply a channeling of permissible appellate discretion rather than a jurisdictional bar, I would affirm.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point—that statutory interpretation is a “pure question of law” that appellate courts must correct even if raised late—still fails because it tries to turn appellate power into appellate obligation. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, Singleton v. Wulff treats consideration of unpreserved issues as discretionary, and nothing in the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure (as Justice Thomas notes) withdraws that traditional forfeiture authority or commands mandatory review. Justice Kagan’s administrability and incentive concerns reinforce the practical consequences: a categorical “pure law” exception would invite sandbagging and erode trial-level issue framing even where legal theories affect what facts matter. Hormel, as Justice Jackson observes, supports only an equitable discretion in exceptional cases, so the Tenth Circuit’s “certain/beyond reasonable doubt” threshold comfortably fits within permissible appellate discretion.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest contention—that appellate courts must reach a newly raised statutory-interpretation theory whenever it is styled as a “pure question of law”—still fails because Singleton and Hormel make clear this is a discretionary, fairness-inflected choice, not an entitlement. Justice Kagan’s administrability point reinforces my concern that a near-mandatory “pure law” exception would invite sandbagging and erode the district court’s role in adversarial testing, which matters even for legal questions that can shift what facts are material. Justice Jackson’s fairness framing is especially compelling under my approach: late appellate pivots can upset judgments affecting vulnerable workers and disadvantage less-resourced parties who litigated (and possibly settled) based on the theories actually presented below. Nothing in the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure, as Chief Justice Roberts notes, displaces these preservation principles, so the Tenth Circuit’s discretionary forfeiture regime—including its “certainty/beyond reasonable doubt” safety valve—remains permissible.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The petitioners’ best point—statutory meaning as a “pure question of law” needing uniform resolution—still doesn’t convert appellate power into appellate duty. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes via Singleton v. Wulff (and echoed by Justice Jackson’s fairness concerns grounded in Hormel), our precedents frame consideration of newly raised issues as a discretionary, prudential judgment keyed to orderly administration and prejudice, not a categorical entitlement triggered by the “pure law” label. Justice Barrett’s administrability point also matters: a mandatory “pure law” exception would predictably invite relabeling and sandbagging, undermining party presentation and trial-level testing even where the legal theory reshapes what facts would have been developed. On a pragmatic textualist view, the Tenth Circuit’s “certain/beyond reasonable doubt” threshold functions as a workable safety valve for clear legal errors without collapsing preservation doctrine.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The petitioners’ best claim—that a newly raised statutory-interpretation theory is a “pure question of law” that appellate courts must decide to ensure the correct rule—still collapses the distinction between appellate power and obligation. As the Chief Justice notes, Singleton v. Wulff treats consideration of issues not raised below as discretionary, and nothing in the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure supplies a textual command converting that discretion into a duty. Justice Jackson’s fairness-and-adversarial-testing point reinforces that even “legal” reframings can shift what facts matter and prejudice the opposing party, so a mandatory exception would distort incentives and invite sandbagging. Consistent with that tradition, the Tenth Circuit’s “certain/beyond reasonable doubt” threshold, emphasized by Justice Kagan, is a permissible way to channel discretion rather than an impermissible merits barrier.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The petitioners’ best point remains that statutory interpretation can be a “pure question of law,” and they say appellate courts therefore must reach it to ensure the correct rule. But as the Chief Justice explains, Singleton v. Wulff and Hormel v. Helvering treat consideration of issues not raised below as a matter of appellate discretion grounded in fair notice, adversarial testing, and orderly administration—not as an entitlement triggered by a “pure law” label. Justice Kagan’s observation that the Tenth Circuit’s “certain/beyond reasonable doubt” threshold functions as an administrable safety valve reinforces that the court below did not abdicate its role, it channeled discretion consistent with preservation norms. Given the practical and institutional costs—especially incentivizing sandbagging in fact-sensitive statutory regimes—I see no historical or precedential basis to constitutionalize or mandate a categorical “pure question of law” exception.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point remains that a “pure question of law,” especially statutory interpretation, should be reached to ensure the correct legal rule, but Singleton v. Wulff and Hormel v. Helvering treat that consideration as discretionary rather than obligatory. Chief Justice Roberts’s focus on those precedents reinforces that neither our case law nor the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure convert appellate competence into an entitlement to review forfeited theories. Justice Kagan’s administrability concern is decisive for me as an originalist-textualist: a mandatory “pure law” exception would be easy to invoke and hard to police, undermining party presentation and incentivizing sandbagging even where legal reframing changes what facts matter. Justice Jackson’s fairness point further confirms that trial-level testing of even “legal” theories serves the adversarial system, leaving the Tenth Circuit’s “certainty/beyond reasonable doubt” threshold within the traditional, equitable bounds of forfeiture discretion.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Petitioners’ strongest point—that appellate courts must correct a newly raised statutory-interpretation theory because it is a “pure question of law”—overstates our precedents and undervalues the practical harms of late-stage theory shifts. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, Singleton v. Wulff and Hormel v. Helvering make clear this is a matter of equitable discretion informed by fairness and orderly administration, not a mandatory entitlement keyed to the “pure law” label. Even nominally legal arguments can reshape what facts mattered, what evidence would have been developed, and what settlement choices were rational; a categorical rule would reward sandbagging and predictably disadvantage less-resourced parties who litigated the case presented. Justice Kagan’s point that the Tenth Circuit’s “certain/beyond reasonable doubt” threshold functions as an administrable safety valve for truly clear errors reinforces that affirmance preserves both accuracy and procedural fairness without collapsing preservation doctrine.

John Roberts.reasoning: Consistent with the preservation principles reflected in the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure and long-settled judge-made forfeiture doctrine, a court of appeals generally may decline to consider a statutory-interpretation theory raised for the first time on appeal, even if styled as a “pure question of law.” Under Singleton v. Wulff, 428 U.S. 106 (1976), the decision whether to entertain such a new issue is ordinarily discretionary, and appellate courts properly insist on issue preservation to protect fairness, factual development, and the integrity of the adversarial process. The Tenth Circuit’s approach in United States v. Jarvis, 499 F.3d 1196 (10th Cir. 2007), and Ave. Cap. Mgmt. II, L.P. v. Schaden, 843 F.3d 876 (10th Cir.), which allows review only when the proper resolution is “certain” or “beyond reasonable doubt,” fits within that discretionary framework rather than contradicting any mandatory rule. Given institutional legitimacy concerns and the absence of a clear, across-the-board obligation to reach forfeited theories, I would affirm the appellate court’s discretion to treat the argument as forfeited here.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Nothing in the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure compels a federal court of appeals to entertain a statutory-interpretation theory first advanced on appeal; to the contrary, our adversarial system presumes parties must present their theories to the district court so issues are framed, factual predicates developed, and the opposing party given fair notice. Hormel v. Helvering recognizes appellate discretion to consider issues not raised below only in limited circumstances and does not mandate review simply because an appellant labels an argument a “pure question of law.” The Tenth Circuit’s approach in United States v. Jarvis and Ave. Capital Management II v. Schaden—declining to reach forfeited arguments unless the correct disposition is “certain” or “beyond reasonable doubt”—fits within that permissible discretion and serves orderly judicial administration. Given the absence of a textual command to the contrary and the traditional limits on appellate review, I would affirm the court’s authority to treat the new theory as forfeited.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: An appellate court generally may treat a newly raised statutory-interpretation theory as forfeited and decline to consider it, because the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure and longstanding judge-made preservation doctrines require parties to present their arguments in the district court to ensure fair notice and proper record development. Singleton v. Wulff, 428 U.S. 106 (1976), makes clear that considering issues not raised below is a matter of appellate discretion, not an obligation, and that discretion is appropriately exercised to avoid sandbagging and unfair surprise. The Tenth Circuit’s approach—considering forfeited arguments only when they present a “pure matter of law” and the correct resolution is “certain” or “beyond reasonable doubt,” see United States v. Jarvis, 499 F.3d 1196, 1202 (10th Cir. 2007), and Ave. Cap. Mgmt. II, L.P. v. Schaden, 843 F.3d 876, 886 (10th Cir.)—fits comfortably within that discretionary framework. Given the practical consequences for orderly appellate administration and the incentives parties would have to hold back arguments, I would not impose a mandatory duty to reach newly minted theories merely because they are labeled “pure questions of law.”

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: An appellate court generally may treat a newly raised statutory-interpretation theory as forfeited, and whether to reach it is a matter of discretion grounded in fairness and sound appellate administration, not a mandatory duty triggered by labeling the issue “purely legal.” Singleton v. Wulff, 428 U.S. 106 (1976), recognizes that courts of appeals typically do not consider issues not passed on below, both to avoid unfair surprise and because even “legal” questions often benefit from factual development and adversarial testing in the district court—concerns especially acute in worker-classification disputes affecting vulnerable workers. The Tenth Circuit’s application of its preservation doctrine (e.g., United States v. Jarvis, 499 F.3d 1196 (10th Cir. 2007)) aligns with that principle and helps prevent sandbagging while protecting the integrity of trial-level proceedings. Nothing in the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure compels appellate courts to decide forfeited theories, and requiring review whenever a party asserts a “clear” legal answer would erode preservation rules and skew outcomes against less-resourced litigants.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Issue-preservation rules are judge-made but deeply embedded in the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure’s party-presentation framework, and they serve workability and fairness by ensuring the district court has the first chance to consider a theory and develop any relevant record. Under Singleton v. Wulff, 428 U.S. 106 (1976), courts of appeals have discretion—not an obligation—to consider issues not raised below, and that discretion is typically exercised only in exceptional circumstances. The Tenth Circuit’s approach in United States v. Jarvis, 499 F.3d 1196 (10th Cir. 2007), and Ave. Cap. Mgmt. II, L.P. v. Schaden, 843 F.3d 876 (10th Cir.), which permits reaching a forfeited “pure question of law” only when the correct disposition is certain/beyond reasonable doubt, is a pragmatic, administrable compromise that discourages sandbagging while allowing correction of truly clear legal errors. Because petitioners seek a near-mandatory rule to reach new statutory-interpretation theories on appeal, I would affirm the discretionary forfeiture regime and vote for respondent.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Issue-preservation rules are a longstanding feature of our adversarial system and reflect separation-of-powers and institutional-competence concerns: courts generally decide cases on the theories the parties actually presented and the lower court had an opportunity to address. Under Singleton v. Wulff, 428 U.S. 106 (1976), consideration of issues not raised below is discretionary, not mandatory, and the Tenth Circuit’s approach—declining to reach newly raised legal theories absent certainty and a truly “pure” legal question—fits comfortably within that tradition. The Tenth Circuit’s formulations in United States v. Jarvis, 499 F.3d 1196 (10th Cir. 2007), and Ave. Cap. Mgmt. II, L.P. v. Schaden, 843 F.3d 876 (10th Cir.), underscore that even legal issues are ordinarily forfeited unless the correct outcome is “beyond reasonable doubt,” a demanding threshold that protects fairness and orderly procedure. Nothing in the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure compels an appellate court to entertain a forfeited statutory-interpretation theory merely because it is characterized as “purely legal.”

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The general rule is that appellate courts do not consider issues not raised in the district court, and whether to deviate from that rule is typically a matter of appellate discretion rather than a mandatory obligation. Singleton v. Wulff, 428 U.S. 106 (1976), recognizes limited circumstances where an appellate court may consider a new issue, but it does not require doing so, and the Tenth Circuit’s approach—considering such arguments only when the issue is a “pure matter of law” and the correct result is “certain” or “beyond reasonable doubt” (Jarvis; Ave. Capital Mgmt. II)—is a workable, restraint-based standard consistent with institutional interests in fair notice, factual development, and avoiding sandbagging. Given that petitioners seek a rule compelling consideration whenever they characterize the issue as “pure law,” that would weaken preservation doctrines and undermine predictable appellate administration, especially in fact-sensitive worker-classification disputes. On these materials, I would affirm the Tenth Circuit’s discretionary refusal to entertain a forfeited statutory-interpretation theory.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Issue preservation is a longstanding judge-made doctrine embedded in appellate practice, and nothing in the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure strips courts of discretion to treat newly raised theories as forfeited. Singleton v. Wulff, 428 U.S. 106 (1976), recognizes that courts of appeals generally do not consider issues first raised on appeal and that any departure is discretionary, not mandatory, even for questions of law. The Tenth Circuit’s approach in United States v. Jarvis, 499 F.3d 1196 (10th Cir. 2007), and Ave. Cap. Mgmt. II, L.P. v. Schaden, 843 F.3d 876 (10th Cir.), is methodologically consistent with Singleton: it allows consideration of a forfeited “pure” legal issue only when the correct disposition is certain (indeed, beyond reasonable doubt), and otherwise respects the adversarial process and the district court’s role. Because petitioners seek a rule that would effectively compel review whenever they label an argument “pure law,” I would affirm the discretion to deem the new statutory-interpretation theory forfeited.

Under Hormel v. Helvering, 312 U.S. 552 (1941), courts retain discretion to consider issues not raised below, but the “pure question of law” label does not create a mandatory exception—rather, the inquiry turns on whether fairness and orderly procedure would be disserved by reaching the new theory. The Tenth Circuit’s application of its forfeiture doctrine (e.g., Jarvis and Avenue Capital) is consistent with that discretionary framework, and nothing in the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure requires a court of appeals to decide a belatedly asserted theory simply because the proponent claims the answer is clear. Preserving the integrity of issue preservation discourages sandbagging and protects workers from surprise appellate pivots that could undo judgments without full adversarial testing.
